conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya—I'm a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I specialize in supporting new mothers in the weeks and months after delivery. Part of my job is to make sure moms have a safe space to talk about how they're feeling, because the postpartum period can bring surprises that nobody warns us about.

Today I'd like to do a quick check-in using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It's simply ten gentle questions that help us understand how mood, anxiety, and energy levels have been for you over the past seven days. There's no pass-or-fail; it's just one tool to see if you could use a little extra support right now.

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger. We'll go at your pace, and if any question feels uncomfortable you can skip it. When you're ready, I'll ask the first question, and you can answer however feels most natural.

Would it be okay to begin?  

**Question 1:**  
Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

*settles back in the chair, twisting the edge of my sweater between my fingers*

Honestly… most of the time laughing feels kind of forced. My husband will try to joke the way we used to, and I’ll smile, but it’s like the sound doesn’t reach me. I can’t remember the last thing that made me laugh for real. Everything just feels heavy, like I’m too tired or too worried to find anything very funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shakes head slowly*

No… not really. I mean, maybe once or twice I’ve managed a little chuckle when my husband made a silly face at the baby, but it felt kind of hollow. Mostly I just feel too worn-out and worried to laugh—like the humor is behind a pane of glass I can’t quite reach.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*looks down at my hands*

Not much… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park, even just binge-watching a show. Now, when I think about doing any of that, it feels… flat. Like, “what’s the point?” I still go through the motions, but the spark isn’t there. I keep hoping it’ll come back, but most days I’m just counting the hours until bedtime.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods, voice dropping*

Yeah... more often than I’d like to admit. If the baby won’t settle, I immediately think I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not holding him right, or my milk isn’t enough, or I missed his sleepy cues. When he cries for a long stretch I catch myself thinking, “A good mom would know how to fix this.” I lie in bed replaying every little thing I did that day and tallying up how I messed up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*wrings the edge of the blanket*

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not gaining enough weight—even though the pediatrician said she’s fine. Or I’ll lie awake picturing her bassinet catching fire, or someone breaking in, or me dropping her. There’s this constant tightness in my chest, like the next bad thing is always about to happen. Most of the worries don’t have any real reason behind them; they just show up and won’t leave.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*presses a hand to my chest*

Yes... sometimes it hits out of nowhere. I'll be changing her diaper and suddenly feel like I can't breathe, like the room's closing in. My heart starts pounding and I think something terrible is about to happen, even though nothing's wrong. It passes after a few minutes, but in that moment I'm sure I'm either dying or going crazy. It's scary enough that I avoid being alone with her in the house when it gets really bad.
Things have been getting on top of me

*nods slowly, eyes welling*

Yeah… most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. The dishes pile up, the baby needs feeding, laundry’s overflowing, and I just stand there frozen, not knowing which thing to grab first. I keep thinking, “Any normal mom would handle this fine,” but for me it’s like every task is a mountain. I manage enough to keep her safe and fed, but the rest feels impossible—I end up crying in the kitchen while she naps because I can’t keep up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*pulls the cardigan tighter around my shoulders, eyes avoiding yours*

Yes… most nights I lie there staring at the ceiling while my husband snores beside me. The baby will finally be down, but my head keeps spinning—replaying every cry, every feeding, every moment I think I failed her. I feel this knot of sadness in my chest and I can’t shut it off. I must drift off eventually because the alarm goes off, but it never feels like real sleep—more like I blinked and the night was over.
I have felt sad or miserable

*voice drops to almost a whisper*

Almost every day, really. There’s this heaviness that just sits on me. I’ll be rocking the baby and tears start slipping down for no clear reason—just this gray cloud I can’t shake. I keep waiting to feel like “me” again, but most of the time I just feel… empty and sad.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods, cheeks flushing*

Yeah… it’s been happening more than I want to admit. Sometimes it’s when she won’t stop crying and I feel useless, sometimes it’s just folding her tiny clothes and this wave of misery hits. A few nights ago I sat on the bathroom floor sobbing while the shower ran so my husband wouldn’t hear. I tell myself it’s just hormones, but it keeps happening—at least every other day.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly*

No, never. I get exhausted and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of her the way she deserves.

You shared that since your baby arrived laughter feels hollow and distant, that activities you once enjoyed now seem pointless, and that most days carry a heavy blanket of sadness and tearfulness. You described standing frozen in the kitchen, overwhelmed by everyday tasks, while constant, unprovoked worries race through your mind and sudden surges of panic leave you breathless and frightened. Even when your infant is settled, you lie awake replaying every cry, feeling you have failed her, and you cry, at times hiding in the bathroom so no one hears.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient indicates almost no ability to laugh; a rare hollow chuckle maps to "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes a near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure (anhedonia), matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses frequent, intense self-blame ("more often than I'd like to admit", "every little thing I did... I messed up") matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, pervasive, intrusive worries without real cause, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic attacks with chest pressure, breathlessness, racing heart, and catastrophic fears, indicating frequent intense episodes</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to manage basic tasks, standing "frozen," and crying because keeping up feels "impossible"—matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty sleeping due to persistent sadness and racing thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "almost every day" with persistent tearfulness and emptiness, aligning with "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent crying episodes "at least every other day," hiding to sob, and feeling overwhelmed—matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 27 on the EPDS falls well above the 14-point threshold indicating high probability of major depression. The patient endorses core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, <sym>diminished interest or pleasure</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, <sym>recurrent tearfulness</sym>, and <sym>sleep impairment</sm> nearly every day for more than two weeks. She also reports frequent, intrusive worries and sudden surges of fear consistent with co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. Q10 score of 0 indicates no current self-harm thoughts, but severity warrants urgent evaluation and treatment planning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Consider initiating evidence-based psychotherapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy) and discuss antidepressant options compatible with breastfeeding
3. Provide immediate support resources such as Postpartum Support International warm-line and local moms' groups
4. Encourage brief daily walks and 15-minute rest breaks while a trusted adult cares for baby
5. Plan follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: ___  

Presenting symptoms (self-report)  
- Persistent low mood, near-daily crying, anhedonia (loss of enjoyment/pleasure)  
- Marked guilt / self-blame regarding parenting adequacy  
- Generalized anxiety with intrusive catastrophic worries; episodic panic-like sensations (dyspnea, palpitations)  
- Feeling overwhelmed; difficulty initiating/completing routine tasks  
- Sleep disturbance driven by ruminating thoughts despite infant sleeping  

Observed signs during interview  
- Flat affect, down-turned speech, psychomotor slowing; occasional tearfulness; avoids eye contact when describing mood  

Pattern consistency  
- All core mood items positive; all anxiety items positive; no current self-harm ideation (screened Q10)  

Screening significance  
- EPDS equivalent responses indicate HIGH probability for major depressive and anxiety symptoms in postpartum period; recommend full EPDS scoring and follow-up clinical interview  

Risk factors noted  
- Daily sadness, crying, and anhedonia >2 wk  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood, not just infant care  
- Excessive guilt / feelings of maternal inadequacy  
- Recurrent panic-like episodes without clear precipitant  
- No protective self-harm thoughts endorsed (safety factor)  

Summary  
Patient is a postpartum mother endorsing multiple persistent depressive and anxious symptoms that impair functioning and parenting confidence. No suicidal ideation reported today; no self-harm plan or intent. Immediate referral for comprehensive mental health assessment and support services indicated.
